title: Seductive Pedagogy v Bullshit Teaching
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that named teaching techniques and codified systems are seductive but easily become empty, because teachers and leaders end up focusing on the named thing rather than on learning. He defines learning as students thinking hard, working hard and remembering more, and says the only reliable guard is to ask of every activity how the students will do those three things. He grounds his stance in impact data, using Progress 8 and similar-school comparisons, and offers his daughter's results as a case study of one. He then applies the test to a published demonstration lesson by David Didau, which he says used many techniques yet may have taught students nothing new, and cites the trust's weak English results as evidence that impact matters more than technique. The tone is combative, and the argument rests on selective comparisons.
points: Naming and codifying techniques helps understanding but is very hard to scale, because teachers focus on the technique instead of learning.
One universal question, how will students think hard, work hard or remember more, keeps any technique honest.
Judging teaching by impact data, such as value-added progress measures, guards against bias in what leaders admire.
A technique-rich demonstration lesson can still fail the learning test if students leave with a thesis statement they already knew.
Asking the learning question about everything compounds into continuous improvement for teachers.
quotes: Regular readers will know that I’m mildly obsessed with impact. So much of what I see in schools and in blogs looks to me as though it will have little or no impact.
Anything you read that codifies, describes, explains and names an aspect of teaching is likely to be kosher. Naming stuff really helps everyone understand what it is and to apply it.
We love these names and systems. Teach Like a Champion has over 60. The Writing Revolution has God knows how many.
Once teachers ask themselves this question about everything they do, they constantly improve. It is the compound interest of teaching.
She isn’t brilliant because of all the fantastic techniques I have taught her. She is brilliant because of this one technique (and obviously all the other qualities she has).
His problem is that he has been seduced by the techniques. We are all seduced by these. But, seductive pedagogy = bullshit teaching.
